why: The replacement examples shifted the model toward inserting boundaries around name/title tokens and around small list elements (helping very short bins ≤3–10 where isolating those tokens raised cohesion), but also nudged it to delay or re-place cuts that previously kept clause cores intact—producing preverbal/predicate fragments and broken list/quantifier frames in mid-length pieces (notably the ≤5 regressions in en_us_1427 and en_us_970). E1 is responsible for the changed name/title segmentation behavior (big wins on en_us_1591), E2 appears to have driven the model to postpone predicate boundaries (explaining the worst examples), and E3 influenced list/quantifier splitting (mixed effect).
lesson: When swapping examples, keep title/name demonstrations and predicate-preservation demonstrations distinct so that examples meant to protect multiword names do not accidentally teach postponing clause-core boundaries or splitting lists.
